title: How To Get Your Misbehaving Class Back On Track
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin proposes a counterintuitive strategy for a class that has drifted off track: rather than talking more, lecturing, or holding a class meeting, the teacher should tighten existing boundaries and ask more, not less, of students. He reasons that a class's slide into misbehavior is evidence they cannot yet handle the current level of freedom, so the appropriate response is to narrow that freedom, whether by restricting talking during transitions, requiring more formal procedures, or adding stricter routines. The specific adjustment matters less than the clear signal it sends: the teacher will protect the class's ability to learn by pulling boundaries in closer whenever necessary. He stresses this must be delivered with calm confidence rather than visible stress or fear, since emotional wavering from the teacher tends to worsen behavior rather than improve it. The piece closes by noting that once good behavior is proven over time, boundaries can be extended back outward, but only as a reward for demonstrated, sustained improvement.
points: When a class drifts off track, the recommended response is to tighten existing boundaries and demand more discipline, not to talk, lecture, or hold a class meeting.
A class's slide into misbehavior signals it cannot yet handle its current level of freedom, so the freedom itself should be narrowed.
The specific adjustment (limiting talking during transitions, adding stricter routines) matters less than the clear signal sent that boundaries will tighten when needed.
Delivering the tightened boundary with calm confidence is essential; visible stress or emotional wavering tends to worsen behavior rather than improve it.
Boundaries can be extended back outward once good behavior is proven and sustained over time, but only as an earned reward for demonstrated improvement.
quotes: When a class gets off track, the tendency is to talk. It’s to rehash, remind, and redo. It’s to circle-up the community, lecture and rebuke.
After all, they’ve just proven that they can’t handle the freedom within the boundaries you currently have. So you must adjust to match their needs.
It doesn’t matter what it is. But limiting existing freedoms, or otherwise requiring more discipline from your students, is the one thing guaranteed to get their attention.

Show fear in the face of losing control, become stressed and emotional, and behavior will get worse, not better. Calmly and confidently tighten your boundaries, however—even in just one little area—and they’ll give in. They’ll acquiesce.
Once you have control and impeccable behavior, proven over time, you can remove the new line. You can extend the boundary and allow more freedom and responsibility.
